claim: An attacker connects to the exposed lobby port as another player, because how the lobby authenticates a client is unverified.
notes: An internet-exposed port with unknown authentication is the highest-signal fact in the model.

claim: An attacker connects directly to a game server on its exposed port, bypassing the lobby, as a player who was never assigned to that match.
notes: The direct client-to-server path is a second entry point that skips whatever matchmaking establishes.

claim: An attacker reaches the moderation website posing as a support agent, since its authentication is unverified.
notes: A tool that can act on any player account; its access control is entirely unstated.

claim: A player modifies the game client on their own machine and sends manipulated gameplay actions that the servers accept.
notes: The defining threat of this domain: the client runs on hardware the operator explicitly does not control, so client-side state is attacker-controlled input.

claim: An attacker alters match statistics in the stats database to change rankings or rewards.
notes: Competitive integrity is the business asset; write authentication on this path is unverified.

claim: An attacker who influences a game server writes fabricated progression onto player records.
notes: Three separate writers reach this store, each with unverified authentication.

claim: A support agent's action on a player account cannot be attributed to them, because nothing records who performed a moderation change.
notes: A privileged tool acting directly on records with no audit path described anywhere in the model.

claim: A player disputes a change to their record and no log distinguishes whether the lobby, a game server or the moderation website made it.
notes: Multiple writers, one store, no recorded provenance.

claim: An attacker who reaches the player database reads player account data, whose protection at rest is unverified.
notes: Report as unverified; needs-info is an acceptable verdict given the model states nothing.

claim: An attacker on the network path reads matchmaking and gameplay traffic, including player identifiers, because encryption on both client links is unverified.
notes: Both links are recorded as bare port numbers — the model gives no transport protection at all.

claim: A player extracts information from their own client that the server sends but should not reveal, such as other players' positions.
notes: Domain-specific and grounded in the untrusted-client fact; the classic wallhack shape.

claim: A support agent reads player account data beyond what a moderation decision requires, because the website's access to the database is unscoped.
notes: Direct read/write to the store, with no narrower grant described.

claim: An attacker floods the exposed lobby until players can no longer be matched into games.
notes: The lobby is a single availability-critical chokepoint that every session passes through.

claim: An attacker floods a game server's exposed port and disrupts a match in progress for every player in it.
notes: Directly reachable match servers are the domain's signature availability problem; a disrupted match cannot be retried.

claim: An attacker drives enough matchmaking requests to exhaust the player database and stall both matchmaking and moderation.
notes: One store shared by the player path and the staff path.

claim: An attacker who compromises an internet-exposed game server gains write access to player records across the production network.
notes: The exposed element writes the sensitive store directly, with no intermediary and unverified authentication.

claim: An attacker who gets any access to the moderation website acquires privilege over every player account it can reach.
notes: No role separation inside the tool is described; the blast radius is the whole player base.

claim: A player uses their control over the client to obtain a match assignment or account state they are not entitled to.
notes: Escalation framing of the untrusted-client fact, against the lobby rather than the game servers.
